positions/nominalism-via-moderna/oneLine: Universals are names, not things; God’s absolute power is limited only by non-contradiction, and the order of salvation rests on God’s freely chosen covenant rather than on necessary natures.
positions/nominalism-via-moderna/coreCla: Only individuals exist; universals are concepts or names (nominalism).
God could have done otherwise by his absolute power (potentia absoluta) but binds himself by his ordained power (potentia ordinata).
Grace and merit work by covenant (pactum): God has promised to give grace to those who do what is in them (facere quod in se est).
Many truths of faith (even God’s unity) cannot be strictly demonstrated; they rest on revelation.
Do not multiply entities without necessity (the "razor").
positions/nominalism-via-moderna/origin: Associated with William of Ockham (c.1320) and developed by Pierre d’Ailly, Jean Gerson and Gabriel Biel (d.1495). In the 15th-century universities the "via moderna" competed with the "via antiqua" of Thomists and Scotists; Luther was trained in it at Erfurt.
positions/nominalism-via-moderna/stronge: It honours God’s freedom and sovereignty against philosophical necessity.
It encouraged empirical attention to individual things and logical rigour.
Its covenant theology gave assurance that God keeps his promises.
Luther and Reformed critics charged its "doing what is in one" with semi-Pelagianism.
Realists said it undermines the knowability of God and of natures, and later critics blame it for modern voluntarism and secularism.
Its fideism separates faith from reason.
positions/nominalism-via-moderna/respons: Defenders note its Augustinian wing (Gregory of Rimini) and argue that the covenant emphasis was itself a theology of grace.
Historians such as Oberman showed its complexity and its role in preparing the Reformation.
positions/nominalism-via-moderna/consequ: Formed Luther’s questions and helped trigger the Reformation.
Influenced covenant theology and early modern science.
positions/renaissance-humanism/oneLine: Return to the sources: renew the Church through eloquent study of Scripture and the Fathers in their original languages and a simple, moral "philosophy of Christ" in place of scholastic subtleties.
positions/renaissance-humanism/coreClaim: The original Hebrew and Greek texts, edited critically, correct the Vulgate and scholastic misreadings.
The early Fathers (Jerome, Origen, Chrysostom) are better guides than late scholastic masters.
Christianity is above all imitation of Christ and inner piety, accessible to lay people.
Good letters (rhetoric, history, philology) serve true theology.
positions/renaissance-humanism/keyTexts/: Valla, Annotations on the New Testament
positions/renaissance-humanism/origin: Grew from 14th-15th-century Italian humanism (Petrarch, Valla) and spread north through John Colet, Thomas More, Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, Cardinal Cisneros (Complutensian Polyglot) and Erasmus, whose Greek New Testament (1516) supplied the text used by Luther and Tyndale.
positions/renaissance-humanism/strongest: It restored accurate texts of Scripture and the Fathers.
It united learning with moral and educational reform.
It equipped both Protestant and Catholic reformers.
Luther charged Erasmus with moralism and a weak doctrine of grace and the will (1524-25).
Scholastic theologians accused humanists of doctrinal amateurism.
Its critical tools could later be turned against traditional doctrines.
positions/renaissance-humanism/responses: Humanists answered that true doctrine grows from the sources themselves and that their critics had abandoned them.
positions/renaissance-humanism/consequen: Greek New Testament and vernacular translations.
positions/protestant-scholasticism/oneLi: The Reformation’s confessions were taught, defended and systematised for universities using refined scholastic method, so that the churches of the Reformation would have a complete, defensible body of divinity.
positions/protestant-scholasticism/coreC: Theology is arranged in loci (topics) and disputations, drawing on Aristotle’s logic and medieval distinctions as tools.
Scripture is the sole principle (principium cognoscendi) of theology, verbally inspired and self-authenticating.
Confessions (Augsburg, Formula of Concord, Belgic, Westminster, Dort) state the faith of the church.
Theology is both theoretical and practical: it aims at God and at living for God.
positions/protestant-scholasticism/origi: Developed from the 1560s (Beza, Zanchi, Chemnitz) and flourished c.1590-1700 (Gerhard, Quenstedt; Polanus, Voetius, Turretin, Owen) in Wittenberg, Jena, Geneva, Leiden, Utrecht and Oxford. Richard Muller and others argue it continued rather than betrayed the Reformers.
positions/protestant-scholasticism/stron: It gave Protestant churches a coherent, teachable doctrine able to answer Catholic, Socinian and Remonstrant critics.
It preserved continuity with the catholic and medieval tradition.
Its works remain a treasury of exegesis and doctrine (e.g. Owen, Turretin).
Pietists and later historians called it "dead orthodoxy": intellectualist and polemical.
Some (e.g. the "Calvin against the Calvinists" thesis) argued it distorted the Reformers by making predestination a central dogma.
Enlightenment critics found its verbal inspiration and confessionalism untenable.
positions/protestant-scholasticism/respo: Muller and others show that orthodoxy was pious and practical, varied, and exegetically serious, and that method is not content.
Its renaissance in recent Reformed and Lutheran scholarship reflects a reassessment.
positions/protestant-scholasticism/conse: Westminster Standards and Formula of Concord as teaching norms.
Princeton theology and modern confessional Protestantism.
positions/puritan-theology/oneLine: Reformed doctrine must be preached plainly, applied to the conscience and lived out in the whole of life: theology is the science of living to God.
positions/puritan-theology/coreClaims/0: The Bible regulates worship and life; the church should be further reformed.
positions/puritan-theology/coreClaims/1: Covenant theology frames God’s dealings with humanity.
positions/puritan-theology/coreClaims/2: Assurance, conversion and sanctification are traced in the soul ("experimental" religion).
positions/puritan-theology/coreClaims/3: Plain-style preaching, family worship, Sabbath and meditation shape a godly commonwealth.
positions/puritan-theology/origin: Arose among English Protestants dissatisfied with the Elizabethan settlement (1560s); its theology was shaped by William Perkins (1590s), William Ames, Richard Sibbes, John Owen, Richard Baxter and, in New England, Thomas Hooker and later Jonathan Edwards.
positions/puritan-theology/strongestArgu: It joined rigorous doctrine to deep pastoral and devotional application.
Its covenant theology and casuistry gave believers practical guidance.
It shaped democratic and educational institutions in Britain and America.
positions/puritan-theology/strongestObje: Critics said it bred introspection and anxiety over assurance.
Its moral rigor and Sabbatarianism were attacked as legalistic; its political wing ended in civil war.
Anglicans argued its regulative principle was unhistorical and divisive.
positions/puritan-theology/responses/0: Puritans pointed to the many consolatory works (Sibbes, The Bruised Reed) and saw introspection as a means to joyful assurance.
positions/puritan-theology/responses/1: Their revival in 20th-century evangelicalism (Lloyd-Jones, Packer) testifies to their pastoral usefulness.
positions/puritan-theology/consequences/: Westminster Assembly; Congregationalist and Baptist churches; New England.
positions/pietist-theology/oneLine: Living faith, new birth and practical holiness matter more than correct doctrine alone; theology should be renewed by Bible study, the priesthood of believers and training of pastors in piety.
positions/pietist-theology/coreClaims/0: Rebirth (Wiedergeburt) and a living relationship with Christ are the heart of Christianity.
positions/pietist-theology/coreClaims/1: Christianity consists more in practice than in knowledge.
positions/pietist-theology/coreClaims/2: Small groups (collegia pietatis) for Bible study express the priesthood of all believers.
positions/pietist-theology/coreClaims/3: Theological training must form godly pastors, and controversy should be conducted with charity.
positions/pietist-theology/coreClaims/4: Faith works through love in education, social care and mission.
positions/pietist-theology/origin: Prepared by Johann Arndt’s True Christianity (1605-10) and launched by Philipp Jakob Spener’s Pia Desideria (1675); institutionalised by August Hermann Francke at Halle (from 1692) and carried into the Moravian renewal by Zinzendorf (1727).
positions/pietist-theology/strongestArgu: It renewed personal faith and lay participation in Lutheran and Reformed churches.
It pioneered Protestant mission, education and social welfare.
It is the spiritual root of Methodism and modern evangelicalism.
positions/pietist-theology/strongestObje: Lutheran orthodox critics (e.g. Valentin Löscher) said it subordinated objective means of grace to subjective experience.
Its emphasis on feeling arguably prepared the way for Schleiermacher’s experiential liberalism.
positions/pietist-theology/responses/0: Pietists replied that they upheld the confessions but wished them lived.
positions/pietist-theology/responses/1: Recent scholarship stresses Pietism’s intellectual and scientific achievements (Bengel’s textual criticism).
positions/pietist-theology/consequences/: Halle and Moravian missions; Methodism; evangelicalism.
Small-group and devotional culture in Protestantism.
positions/enlightenment-deism/oneLine: Reason is the judge of revelation: true religion consists of what reason can know (God, morality, immortality), and anything contrary to reason, or in the radical Deist view anything beyond it, must be rejected.
positions/enlightenment-deism/coreClaims: A universal natural religion (one God, virtue, future rewards) is available to all by reason.
Revelation can at most republish natural religion; miracles and mysteries are doubtful.
Priestcraft and dogma corrupted Jesus’ simple moral teaching.
Religious toleration follows from the limits of certainty.
positions/enlightenment-deism/keyTexts/3: Tindal, Christianity as Old as the Creation (1730)
positions/enlightenment-deism/keyTexts/4: Kant, Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason (1793)
positions/enlightenment-deism/origin: Grew in England after the wars of religion (Herbert of Cherbury 1624; Toland 1696; Tindal 1730), then in France (Voltaire) and Germany (Reimarus, Lessing, Kant). Moderate "rational supernaturalists" such as Locke and Samuel Clarke defended revelation on rational grounds.
positions/enlightenment-deism/strongestA: It answered religious warfare with a call to tolerance and shared reason.
It forced theology to give reasons and to face historical questions about the Bible.
It stressed ethics as the test of religion.
positions/enlightenment-deism/strongestO: Joseph Butler’s Analogy (1736) argued that nature is as mysterious as revelation, so Deist objections cut both ways.
Hume showed that reason could not easily establish even natural religion.
Orthodox and evangelical critics said it reduced Christianity to morality and removed grace, Christ and redemption.
positions/enlightenment-deism/responses/: Deists claimed to restore the pure religion of Jesus, which Jefferson tried to extract in his Bible.
positions/enlightenment-deism/consequenc: Unitarianism; historical criticism of the Bible (Reimarus’ fragments, 1774-78).
Separation of church and state ideals.
